read.sections.0.text.source: A tradition is a practice that people share and repeat over time. It can be a meal, a song, a game, a skill or a celebration. Many traditions mark an important time of year. Nowruz is a spring new year. Millions of people celebrate it in many countries, from south-east Europe to Central Asia. People clean, share special meals and enjoy music and dance. The community meal in the evidence is a tradition too. The elder says it matters because people meet, teach and welcome each other.
read.sections.0.text.back: A tradition is something people do together and repeat over a long time. It may be food, songs, games, skills or celebrations. Many traditions mark important times of the year. Nowruz is the new year's day in spring. Millions of people in many countries celebrate it, from south-eastern Europe to Central Asia. People clean their homes, eat special food together and enjoy music and dancing. The community feast in the evidence is a tradition too. The elder says it matters because people meet, teach each other and welcome one another.
read.sections.0.text.note: Nowruz = นาวรูซ (โนรูซ and เนารูซ also appear in Thai writing; please choose one). The checker warns that "Nowruz" no longer appears in Latin letters: it is a real festival, so it takes a Thai spelling like the other real names.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: A tradition is a thing people do again and again, for many years. It can be a meal, a song or a game. Many traditions mark a special time of year. Nowruz is a new year in spring. People in many lands celebrate it. They clean, share food and dance. The meal in the evidence is a tradition too. The elder says it helps people meet, teach and welcome others.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: A tradition is something people do again and again over many years. It may be food, songs or games. Many traditions mark special times of the year. Nowruz is the new year in spring. People in many lands celebrate this day. They clean, eat together and dance. The feast in the evidence is a tradition too. The elder says it helps people meet, teach each other and welcome others.

read.sections.1.text.source: Many traditions help older people pass knowledge to younger people. This is called transmission. In Korea, families and neighbours make kimchi together in late autumn. This tradition is called kimjang. They share the kimchi between homes and swap ideas. In North Africa, people learn to make couscous by watching and copying others. They eat it together at big family and community events. In Tonga, large groups perform the lakalaka. It is a dance with sung speeches about history and values. In the evidence, a young helper learns to make the bread and wants to teach it next year.
read.sections.1.text.back: Many traditions help older generations pass knowledge to younger ones. This is called transmission. In Korea, families and neighbours make kimchi together in late autumn. This tradition is called kimjang. They share kimchi between homes and exchange ideas. In North Africa, people learn to make couscous by watching and copying others. They eat couscous together at big family and community events. In Tonga, large groups perform the lakalaka, a dance with singing that tells of history and values. In the evidence, the young helper learned to make bread and wants to teach others next year.
read.sections.1.text.note: kimchi = กิมจิ, kimjang = กิมจัง, couscous = คูสคูส, lakalaka = ลาคาลาคา, Tonga = ตองกา. "sung speeches" = การขับร้องเล่าเรื่อง; check it describes lakalaka fairly. The simpler text explains couscous as "อาหารที่ทำจากเม็ดแป้งเล็กๆ" (the English says "tiny grains").

read.sections.1.simpler.source: Traditions help older people teach younger people. This is called transmission. In Korea, people make kimchi from vegetables. They make it in a big group in autumn. Then they share it. In North Africa, people learn to cook couscous. It is a dish of tiny grains. They watch others and copy them. In Tonga, big groups sing and dance the lakalaka. The songs tell about the past. In the evidence, a young helper learns to make bread.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: Traditions help older generations teach younger ones. This is called transmission. In Korea, people make kimchi from vegetables. They make it in big groups in autumn, then share the kimchi. In North Africa, people learn to make couscous. Couscous is a food made from small grains of flour/dough. They watch others and then copy. In Tonga, large groups sing and dance the lakalaka. The songs tell stories of the past. In the evidence, the young helper learned to make bread.

read.sections.2.heading.source: Traditions can change and still matter
read.sections.2.heading.back: Traditions can change and still matter

read.sections.2.text.source: Traditions are not frozen in the past. People adapt them to fit new times. This year, the meal adds vegetarian dishes and starts earlier, so more people can take part. The new neighbour says the earlier time means they can come for the first time. A change like this can help a tradition keep its purpose: to meet, teach and welcome. It helps when the group talks about what to keep and what to change. Not everyone in a community follows the same traditions or gives them the same meaning. No tradition is better than another.
read.sections.2.text.back: Traditions are not frozen in the past. People adapt traditions to fit changing times. This year the feast added vegetarian food and started earlier, so more people could come. The new neighbour says starting earlier let them come for the first time. Changes like this help a tradition keep its purpose: meeting, teaching each other and welcoming. It also helps when a group talks about what to keep and what to change. Not everyone in a community follows the same traditions or gives them the same meaning. No tradition is better than another.
read.sections.2.text.note: Second pass: "to fit new times" was ยุคสมัยใหม่ (reads as "the modern era"); now ยุคสมัยที่เปลี่ยนไป (changing times).

read.sections.2.simpler.source: Traditions do not stay the same forever. People adapt them to fit new times. This year, the meal has food with no meat. It also starts earlier. Now a new neighbour can come. So the meal keeps its purpose. It still helps people meet and welcome others. The group can talk about what to keep. People in a group may not all do the same things. No tradition is better than another.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: Traditions do not stay the same forever. People adapt traditions to fit new times. This year the feast has food with no meat. It also starts earlier. Now the new neighbour can come. So the feast still keeps its purpose. It still helps people meet and welcome others. A group can talk about what to keep. People in the same group may not do everything the same way. No tradition is better than another.

write.example.source: The purpose of the meal is to meet, teach and welcome people. The elder says this is why the gathering matters. One change is that the meal now starts earlier. This could help because a new neighbour can come for the first time. The vegetarian dishes may also let more people eat together. So the changes can help the meal keep its purpose. The organisers should also ask people which parts matter most to them.

The organisers should also ask which part matters most to people.

watch.summary.source: This video was made at the Smithsonian Folklife Festival in Washington, D.C., in the United States. The festival invites people from many communities. They share their music, dance, crafts and food. In the video, people at the festival talk about why sharing culture matters. Sharing culture helps people learn about each other. It helps them see the world in new ways. It can help people stay strong in hard times and feel joy in good times. Each speaker gives their own view. No one person speaks for a whole culture. When you share with respect, you listen to the people who practise a tradition. You also give them credit.
watch.summary.back: This video was filmed at the Smithsonian Folklife Festival in Washington, D.C., United States. The festival invites people from many communities. They share their music, dance, crafts and food. In the video, people at the festival talk about why sharing culture matters. Sharing culture helps people learn about each other, helps them see the world in new ways, helps people be strong in hard times and be happy in good times. Each speaker gives their own view. No single person can speak for a whole culture. When you share respectfully, you listen to the people who practise the tradition and give them credit.
watch.summary.note: "Smithsonian Folklife Festival" kept in Latin letters as เทศกาล Smithsonian Folklife; Washington, D.C. = กรุงวอชิงตัน ดี.ซี. (contains the abbreviation ดี.ซี., which is how the city is normally named; check it reads aloud well). "give them credit" = ให้เครดิต.
